n: Don’t brag about tomorrow, because you don’t know what a day will bring. James teaches the same humility about our plans.

f.w: Boast not thyself of to morrow

n: Let others praise you, not your own mouth—a stranger, not your own lips.
Stones and sand are heavy, but the trouble a fool’s anger causes is heavier still.

f.g: His provocation, the vexation he causes.

n: Anger is cruel and fury overwhelming, but jealousy is even harder to withstand.
Honest correction spoken openly is better than love that never shows itself.

f.w: Open rebuke is better than secret love

n: A friend’s honest words may hurt, but they can be trusted; an enemy’s kisses are fake. Think of Judas’s kiss.

f.w: Faithful are the wounds of a friend
the kisses of an enemy are deceitful

n: When you’re full, even honey is unappealing; when you’re hungry, even bitter food tastes sweet. Need changes how we value things.

f.g: loatheth = tramples on, refuses with disgust.

n: A person who wanders from home is like a bird that strays from its nest—vulnerable and restless.
Perfume and oil delight the heart, and so does a friend’s heartfelt advice.

f.g: Fragrant oils were used to refresh guests.
Advice that comes from the heart.

n: Don’t abandon old family friends. When trouble hits, a nearby neighbor may help more than a distant relative.

f.w: better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off

n: Be wise, my child, and make me glad, so I can answer anyone who criticizes me. A child’s good life vindicates the parent’s teaching.

f.g: Anyone who insults or criticizes me.

n: The prudent see danger and take refuge; the naive keep going and suffer. (Repeats 22:3.)

f.w: A prudent man foreseeth the evil

n: Take the coat of someone who guarantees a stranger’s debt. (Nearly repeats 20:16.)
A loud blessing shouted early in the morning will be taken as a curse. Overdone or badly timed praise can seem fake or annoying.

f.g: At an inconvenient hour, when people are still sleeping.

n: A quarrelsome spouse is like a constant drip on a rainy day.
Trying to restrain her is like trying to hold back the wind or grab oil with your hand.

f.g: bewrayeth = betrays, reveals; the oil can’t be grasped and gives itself away.

n: As iron sharpens iron, one person sharpens another. Good friends improve each other through honest interaction.

f.g: Face—here the whole person, their character.

n: Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and whoever faithfully serves his master will be honored.

f.w: he that waiteth on his master shall be honoured

n: As water reflects a face, a person’s heart reflects who they really are—or, others can see themselves in us.

f.w: As in water face answereth to face
f.g: Like a reflection in still water.

n: Death and the grave are never satisfied, and neither are human eyes—we always want more.

f.g: Sheol and Abaddon—the grave and the place of destruction.

f.w: the eyes of man are never satisfied

n: As fire tests silver and gold, praise tests a person. How we handle praise reveals our character.

f.g: fining pot = a crucible for refining.

n: Even if you grind a fool like grain in a mortar, you won’t get the folly out of him. Stubborn folly resists even harsh measures.

f.g: A bowl where grain was pounded with a club (pestle).

n: Verses 23–27 are a short poem about farming. Know the condition of your flocks and pay attention to your herds.

f.g: Literally “the face of your flocks”—know each animal.

n: Riches don’t last forever, and even a crown doesn’t pass securely to every generation. Steady, careful stewardship matters more.
When the hay is cut and new growth appears, and the hillside grasses are gathered, God’s provision shows itself.

f.g: Grasses and plants gathered from the hillsides.

n: Lambs provide wool for clothing, and goats can be sold to buy a field.

f.g: Goats can be sold to buy land.

n: There will be plenty of goat’s milk for your family and your servants. Faithful stewardship of what you have leads to lasting provision.
